title: Static Members
relevance: Interviewers use static members to check whether candidates understand class-level shared state, lifetime, and the constraints on static functions versus instance methods in C++.

phases.goal: Establish that static members belong to the class, are shared across instances, and have program lifetime.

must_hit.point: Static members belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances, existing even if no objects have been created.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts object members with class-owned statics that are shared and usable without instances.

must_hit.point: A static data member has only one copy in the entire program and lives for the whole program: created at start and destroyed at termination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says one shared copy regardless of how many objects exist, with program-long lifetime.

must_hit.point: Static members are stored in the data segment (or BSS if uninitialised), not on the stack or heap alongside object instances.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names data/BSS segment and explicitly rejects stack/heap-with-object storage.

probes: How do static members differ from normal class members in ownership, sharing, and lifetime?

hints.1: Think about who owns the member: each object, or the class.
hints.2: Consider how many copies exist and when that storage is created and destroyed.
hints.3: Static members are class-owned, one shared copy for the whole program, not per-object stack/heap fields.

phases.goal: Explain declaration versus definition, in-class initialisation rules, and static function access limits.

must_hit.point: Historically a static member must be declared inside the class but defined and initialised outside the class in a single source file.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows in-class declaration plus out-of-class Class::member = value definition.

must_hit.point: C++17 inline static allows defining and initialising static members directly inside the class, avoiding a separate out-of-class definition.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions C++17 inline static in-class definition as the modern alternative.

must_hit.point: A static member function has no this pointer, so it can only directly access other static members and cannot read or modify non-static members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links no this to static-only access and gives an error for touching instance fields.

must_hit.point: Older standards allow in-class init of const static integral types; constexpr static members are implicitly inline and must be initialised in the class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes const integral in-class init from non-integral types, and states constexpr static is implicitly inline.

probes: How do you declare, define, and initialise a static data member, and what can a static member function access?

hints.1: Separate the blueprint (declaration) from the actual memory allocation (definition).
hints.2: Cover classic out-of-class definition, C++17 inline static, and the no-this rule for static functions.
hints.3: Declare in class, define outside unless inline static / allowed const integral or constexpr static; static functions may touch only other statics.

phases.goal: Choose clear access style and avoid unsafe cross-translation-unit static dependencies.

must_hit.point: Prefer accessing static members via the class name and scope resolution (Class::member) over object access, because it communicates that the member is static.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says object access works but Class::member is strongly preferred for clarity.

must_hit.point: Avoid cross-file dependencies between static variables; if needed, wrap the static in a function that returns a reference (Construct On First Use).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the static initialisation order problem and the function-local reference idiom as the safe pattern.

probes: How should you access statics, and what goes wrong when statics in different .cpp files depend on each other?

hints.1: Think about what the call site communicates: instance state or class state.
hints.2: Recall that the standard does not guarantee static init order across translation units.
hints.3: Prefer Class::member; avoid cross-file static deps, or use Construct On First Use returning a reference.

phases.goal: Apply static members to instance tracking, utilities, factories, and Singleton-style access.

must_hit.point: A classic use is an object counter: a shared static count updated in constructors/destructors, read via a static getter.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes increment/decrement of a shared count and a static function returning the active count.

must_hit.point: Static functions are typically used for utility groupings, instance management, factory methods, and as the global access method in the Singleton pattern.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists utilities/factories/Singleton static access rather than only mentioning a counter.

must_hit.point: In Python, the equivalents are a class variable for static data and a method decorated with @staticmethod for a static member function.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps C++ static data to class variables and static functions to @staticmethod.

probes: Give a concrete example of using static members to track live instances, and name other common design uses.

hints.1: Start with something every object must update on create and destroy.
hints.2: Add a static reader, then mention factories or Singleton-style Class::getInstance.
hints.3: Shared counter in ctor/dtor plus static getter; also utilities, factories, and Singleton access.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both can reach a static member, but Class::member is strongly preferred because it makes the class-level ownership obvious at the call site.

tradeoffs.topic: Out-of-class definition vs C++17 inline static
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Classic C++ requires a single out-of-class definition for allocation; C++17 inline static lets you define and initialise in-class and skip the separate definition.

tradeoffs.topic: Cross-file static dependency vs Construct On First Use
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Depending on another translation unit's static risks the static initialisation order fiasco; wrapping the static in a function that returns a reference initialises on first use and avoids that order hazard.

gotchas.trap: Assuming static member functions can use const or virtual like ordinary member functions.
gotchas.correction: const qualifies this, which static functions do not have, so const is meaningless; virtual needs an object's vtable, which is impossible without an instance.

gotchas.trap: Letting one static variable's initialisation depend on another static from a different .cpp file.
gotchas.correction: Init order across translation units is unspecified (static initialisation order fiasco); avoid the dependency or use Construct On First Use.

gotchas.trap: Trying to initialise a non-integral const static (for example const static std::string) in-class under older rules, or having a static function touch non-static fields.
gotchas.correction: Only const static integral types had the old in-class init exception; non-integrals need out-of-class definition, and static functions may only directly access other statics.
